Possible Sizes of Sumsets

Isaac Rajagopal
Abstract

Nathanson introduced the range of cardinalities of hh-fold sumsets

ℛ⁡(h,k)≔{|h​A|:A⊂ℤ​ and ​|A|=k}.\mathcal{R}(h,k)\coloneq\{|hA|:A\subset\mathbb{Z}\text{ and }|A|=k\}.

Following a remark of Erdős and Szemerédi that determined the form of ℛ⁡(h,k)\mathcal{R}(h,k) when h=2h=2, Nathanson asked what the form of ℛ⁡(h,k)\mathcal{R}(h,k) is for arbitrary h,k∈ℕh,k\in\mathbb{N}. For h∈ℕh\in\mathbb{N}, we prove there is some constant kh∈ℕk_{h}\in\mathbb{N} such that if k>khk>k_{h}, then ℛ⁡(h,k)\mathcal{R}(h,k) is the entire interval [h​k−h+1,(h+k−1h)]\left[hk-h+1,\binom{h+k-1}{h}\right] except for a specified set of (h−12)\binom{h-1}{2} numbers. Moreover, we show that one can take k3=2k_{3}=2.

1 Introduction

Let A⊂ℤA\subset\mathbb{Z} be a set of integers. For h∈ℕh\in\mathbb{N}, write

h​A≔{a1+⋯+ah:ai∈A}hA\coloneq\{a_{1}+\cdots+a_{h}:a_{i}\in A\}

to denote the hh-fold sumset of AA. Note that the aia_{i} need not be distinct. Nathanson defined the set ℛ⁡(h,k)\mathcal{R}(h,k) of the possible sizes of these hh-fold sumsets when |A|=k|A|=k.

Definition 1.1 ([Nat25c]).

Let h,k∈ℕh,k\in\mathbb{N}. Define the range of cardinalities of hh-fold sumsets

ℛ⁡(h,k)≔{|h​A|:A⊂ℤ​ and ​|A|=k}.\mathcal{R}(h,k)\coloneq\{|hA|:A\subset\mathbb{Z}\text{ and }|A|=k\}.

Nathanson [Nat25c] posed the problem of determining the exact values in ℛ⁡(h,k)\mathcal{R}(h,k) for arbitrary h,k∈ℕh,k\in\mathbb{N}. In this paper, we will determine the form of ℛ⁡(h,k)\mathcal{R}(h,k) for fixed h∈ℕh\in\mathbb{N} and large kk, and for h=3h=3 and all k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, specifically answering Nathanson’s Problems 8 and 9 in [Nat25c].

The first work related to ℛ⁡(h,k)\mathcal{R}(h,k) was by Erdős and Szemerédi [ES83], who remarked that “it is easy to see that” ℛ⁡(2,k)=[2​k−1,(k+12)]\mathcal{R}(2,k)=\left[2k-1,\binom{k+1}{2}\right] for all k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}. Nathanson [Nat25c] determined the exact form of ℛ⁡(h,3)\mathcal{R}(h,3) for any h∈ℕh\in\mathbb{N}. Nathanson’s recent program has involved finding specific values in ℛ⁡(h,k)\mathcal{R}(h,k) and studying the frequency with which certain sumset sizes show up, with particular attention to k=4k=4 [Nat25a, Nat25b, Nat25c, Nat26a, Nat26b, O’B25]. With fixed h>2h>2 and kk increasing, the problem of determining ℛ⁡(h,k)\mathcal{R}(h,k) remained fully open.

For real numbers aa and bb, let [a,b][a,b] denote the interval of integers from ⌈a⌉\lceil a\rceil to ⌊b⌋\lfloor b\rfloor, including endpoints. It is not hard to show [Nat96, Theorem 1.3] that

ℛ⁡(h,k)⊆[h​k−h+1,(h+k−1h)],\mathcal{R}(h,k)\subseteq\left[hk-h+1,\binom{h+k-1}{h}\right], (1.1)

and that the endpoints of this interval are achieved by the arithmetic progression A=[0,k−1]A=[0,k-1] and the geometric series A={1,h+1,(h+1)2,…,(h+1)k−1}A=\{1,h+1,(h+1)^{2},\ldots,(h+1)^{k-1}\}. Let m=h​k−h+1m=hk-h+1. Tang–Xing [TX21] and Schinina [Sch26] independently found that there are no elements of ℛ⁡(h,k)\mathcal{R}(h,k) in [m+1,m+h−2][m+1,m+h-2]. Tang–Xing also found that there are no elements of ℛ⁡(h,k)\mathcal{R}(h,k) in [m+h+1,m+2​h−3]∪[m+2​h+1,m+3​h−4][m+h+1,m+2h-3]\cup[m+2h+1,m+3h-4] if k≥5k\geq 5. We extend this trio of intervals into a set of min⁡{h,k}−2\min\{h,k\}-2 intervals, which we call Δh,k\Delta_{h,k} because they geometrically form a triangle when h≤kh\leq k, as shown in Figure 1.

Definition 1.2.

Let m=h​k−h+1m=hk-h+1. Then define

Δh,k≔⋃ℓ=0min⁡{h,k}−3[m+ℓ​h+1,m+ℓ​h+(h−2−ℓ)].\Delta_{h,k}\coloneq\bigcup_{\ell=0}^{\min\{h,k\}-3}[m+\ell h+1,m+\ell h+(h-2-\ell)].
Theorem 1.3.

For all h,k∈ℕh,k\in\mathbb{N}, we have

ℛ⁡(h,k)∩Δh,k=∅.\mathcal{R}(h,k)\cap\Delta_{h,k}=\emptyset.

Figure 1 shows an illustrated example of the points ruled out by Theorem 1.3. Tang–Xing’s [TX21] theorem describes the intervals in Δh,k\Delta_{h,k} with ℓ=0\ell=0 and ℓ=1\ell=1 and ℓ=2\ell=2, which are the uppermost three rows of the triangle in Figure 1, while Schinina’s [Sch26] theorem describes the interval in Δh,k\Delta_{h,k} with ℓ=0\ell=0, which is the uppermost row of the triangle in Figure 1. Our main theorem states that for general hh and large kk, all other numbers in the bounding interval outside Δh,k\Delta_{h,k} are in ℛ⁡(h,k)\mathcal{R}(h,k).

Theorem 1.4.

Fix h∈ℕh\in\mathbb{N}. There exists a constant kh∈ℕk_{h}\in\mathbb{N} such that if k>khk>k_{h}, then

ℛ⁡(h,k)=[h​k−h+1,(h+k−1h)]∖Δh,k.\mathcal{R}(h,k)=\left[hk-h+1,\binom{h+k-1}{h}\right]\setminus\Delta_{h,k}.
Remark 1.5.

Tracking constants in our proof shows that one can take kh≤220​h2k_{h}\leq 2^{20h^{2}}. We have not attempted to optimize this quantity further because it appears to be quite far from the truth.

Numerical experiments for small hh and kk suggest that perhaps the conclusion of Theorem 1.4 holds for all k>hk>h.

Conjecture 1.6.

Let h∈ℕh\in\mathbb{N}, and let k>hk>h. Then

ℛ⁡(h,k)=[h​k−h+1,(h+k−1h)]∖Δh,k.\mathcal{R}(h,k)=\left[hk-h+1,\binom{h+k-1}{h}\right]\setminus\Delta_{h,k}.

When k<h−1k<h-1, the conclusion of Conjecture 1.6 never holds; this follows from results of Lev [Lev96]. See Section 5.2 for a discussion of what happens when k≤hk\leq h.

For any fixed hh, Theorem 1.4 reduces Conjecture 1.6 to a finite problem, albeit a computationally intensive one. We are able to prove that k3=2k_{3}=2 suffices, which implies Conjecture 1.6 when h=3h=3; note that Δ3,k={3​k−1}\Delta_{3,k}=\{3k-1\}.

Theorem 1.7.

If k>2k>2, then

ℛ⁡(3,k)={3​k−2}∪[3​k,(k+23)].\mathcal{R}(3,k)=\{3k-2\}\cup\left[3k,\binom{k+2}{3}\right].

In contrast with previous work, our proofs of Theorem 1.4 and Theorem 1.7 are nonconstructive; for a single desired sumset size, our proof does not give an explicit construction attaining it. Instead, we use continuity-type arguments to prove existence. We construct a sequence of sets AiA_{i} such that, even though the quantities |h​Ai||hA_{i}| vary non-monotonically, we can guarantee that the entire set {|h​Ai|}\{|hA_{i}|\} is an interval. To study |h​A||hA|, we also study the distribution of the tuples (|A|,|2​A|,|3​A|,…,|h​A|)(|A|,|2A|,|3A|,\ldots,|hA|) for various kk-element sets AA. Even though we do not characterize exactly which tuples are possible, we extract enough structural information to characterize the possible values of |h​A||hA|. This opens up fruitful directions for new research, to control these tuples more precisely. Another key part of our construction is combining dense sets, meaning sets with small doubling, and sparse sets, which look like Sidon sets or BhB_{h} sets, to get sets in the middle.

Remark 1.8.

We can also define N⁡(h,k)N(h,k) to be the minimal N≥0N\geq 0 such that

ℛ⁡(h,k)={|h​A|:A⊂[0,N]​ and ​|A|=k}.\mathcal{R}(h,k)=\{|hA|:A\subset[0,N]\text{ and }|A|=k\}.

By general considerations, Nathanson [Nat26b, Theorem 8] proved that N⁡(h,k)≤4​(8​h)k−1N(h,k)\leq 4(8h)^{k-1}. Recently, ChatGPT 5.5 Pro, with light prompting from Timothy Gowers and the author, optimized the constructions in this paper to prove that N⁡(h,k)N(h,k) is polynomial in kk. In a recent blog post [GR26], Gowers and the author describe the ChatGPT construction and intuition for why it works, detail how to show the explicit bound N⁡(h,k)≤k10​h3N(h,k)\leq k^{10h^{3}} for kk sufficiently large, and provide the fully ChatGPT-written proof that N⁡(h,k)N(h,k) is polynomial in kk.

1.1 Roadmap

In Section 2, we prove Theorem 1.3 by using results from [Lev96] which generalize Freiman’s 3​k−33k-3 theorem to control the sizes of sumsets from the diameter of sets. We then prove Theorem 1.7 before Theorem 1.4 because the proof of Theorem 1.7 contains simpler versions of some of the ideas in the proof of Theorem 1.4. In Section 3, we prove Theorem 1.7 using a nonconstructive inductive argument involving understanding the possible tuples (|2​A|,|3​A|)(|2A|,|3A|) for all sets A⊂ℤA\subset\mathbb{Z} with |A|=k|A|=k. The bulk of the paper is in Section 4, where we prove Theorem 1.4. This is done using two separate constructions: In Section 4.2, we construct sets AA with smaller values of |h​A||hA| using a partially inductive construction; in Section 4.3, we construct sets AA with larger values of |h​A||hA| by combining dense sets that resemble arithmetic progressions with sparse sets that resemble geometric sequences. Section 5 discusses possible future directions of research and open problems.

2 Ruling out Numbers from ℛ⁡(h,k)\mathcal{R}(h,k)

In this section, we will prove Theorem 1.3 quickly using results from [Lev96]. We begin by defining the diameter of a set AA.

Definition 2.1.

For A⊂ℤA\subset\mathbb{Z} finite, define its diameter diam⁡(A)\mathrm{diam}(A) as 1 less than the minimum length of an arithmetic progression containing AA.

Since affine linear transformations of AA preserve both |h​A||hA| and diam⁡(A)\mathrm{diam}(A), we may always assume that min⁡(A)=0\min(A)=0 and max⁡(A)=diam⁡(A)\max(A)=\mathrm{diam}(A) and gcd⁡(A)=1\gcd(A)=1. Write A={0,a1,…,ak−1}A=\{0,a_{1},\ldots,a_{k-1}\} with ai<ai+1a_{i}<a_{i+1} and gcd⁡(a1,…,ak−1)=1\gcd(a_{1},\ldots,a_{k-1})=1. Let d≔ak−1=diam⁡(A)d\coloneq a_{k-1}=\mathrm{diam}(A). Now, we state a result from [Lev96] about how diam⁡(A)\mathrm{diam}(A) controls |h​A||hA|.

Theorem 2.2 ([Lev96]).

For any A⊂ℤA\subset\mathbb{Z} with |A|=k≥2|A|=k\geq 2 and d=diam⁡(A)d=\mathrm{diam}(A) and h≥2h\geq 2,

|h​A|≥|(h−1)​A|+min⁡{d,h⁡(k−2)+1}.|hA|\geq|(h-1)A|+\min\{d,h(k-2)+1\}. (2.1)

Let q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N} satisfy q⁡(k−2)+1≤d≤(q+1)​(k−2)+1q(k-2)+1\leq d\leq(q+1)(k-2)+1. By applying (2.1) inductively,

|h​A|≥|h⁡{0,1,2,…,k−2,d}|={h⁡(h+1)2​(k−2)+h+1 if ​h≤qq⁡(q+1)2​(k−2)+q+1+(h−q)​d if ​h≥q.|hA|\geq|h\{0,1,2,\ldots,k-2,d\}|=\begin{cases}\frac{h(h+1)}{2}(k-2)+h+1&\text{ if }h\leq q\\ \frac{q(q+1)}{2}(k-2)+q+1+(h-q)d&\text{ if }h\geq q.\end{cases} (2.2)

When h=2h=2 and q=1q=1, (2.2) becomes Freiman’s 3​k−33k-3 theorem (see [Nat96, Theorem 1.13]). Using Theorem 2.2, we can prove Theorem 1.3.

Proof of Theorem 1.3.

If h∈{1,2}h\in\{1,2\} or k∈{1,2}k\in\{1,2\} then Δh,k=∅\Delta_{h,k}=\emptyset, so let h,k≥3h,k\geq 3. Let AA be a set of kk integers, with d=diam⁡(A)d=\mathrm{diam}(A). It suffices to show that |h​A|∉Δh,k|hA|\not\in\Delta_{h,k}.

Case 1: d<2​k−3d<2k-3.

Let ℓ∈[0,min⁡{h,k}−3]\ell\in[0,\min\{h,k\}-3]. Suppose |h​A|≥m+ℓ​h+1=h⁡(k−1+ℓ)+2|hA|\geq m+\ell h+1=h(k-1+\ell)+2. For cardinality reasons, h​A⊈[0,h⁡(k−1+ℓ)]hA\not\subseteq[0,h(k-1+\ell)], so d≥k−ℓd\geq k-\ell. In Theorem 2.2, we have q=1q=1 so therefore (2.2) becomes

|h​A|≥k+(h−1)​d≥k+(h−1)​(k−ℓ)=m+ℓ​h+(h−ℓ−1).|hA|\geq k+(h-1)d\geq k+(h-1)(k-\ell)=m+\ell h+(h-\ell-1).

Therefore, |h​A||hA| is not in the interval [m+ℓ​h+1,m+ℓ​h+(h−ℓ−2)][m+\ell h+1,m+\ell h+(h-\ell-2)]. So |h​A|∉Δh,k|hA|\not\in\Delta_{h,k}.

Case 2: d≥2​k−3d\geq 2k-3.

Theorem 2.2, specifically (2.1), implies that |i​A|−|(i−1)​A|≥2​k−3|iA|-|(i-1)A|\geq 2k-3 for all i≥2i\geq 2. Applying this h−1h-1 times and using that |A|=k|A|=k, then

|h​A|≥k+(h−1)​(2​k−3)=2​h​k−3​h−k+3.|hA|\geq k+(h-1)(2k-3)=2hk-3h-k+3. (2.3)

As ℓ≤k−3\ell\leq k-3 for all elements of Δh,k\Delta_{h,k},

max⁡(Δh,k)≤m+(k−3)​h+(h−2−(k−3))=2​h​k−3​h−k+2.\max(\Delta_{h,k})\leq m+(k-3)h+(h-2-(k-3))=2hk-3h-k+2.

Therefore, |h​A|>max⁡(Δh,k)|hA|>\max(\Delta_{h,k}) so |h​A|∉Δh,k|hA|\not\in\Delta_{h,k}. ∎

3 Finding ℛ⁡(3,k)\mathcal{R}(3,k)

We begin by defining a useful graph, which we will use to formulate our inductive hypothesis.

Definition 3.1.

Define the graph representation of a set A⊂ℤA\subset\mathbb{Z} as g⁡(A)≔(|2​A|,|3​A|)g(A)\coloneq(|2A|,|3A|). Define the kk-sumset graph 𝒢k\mathcal{G}_{k} to have vertex set

Vk={g⁡(A):A⊂ℤ​ and ​|A|=k}.V_{k}=\{g(A):A\subset\mathbb{Z}\text{ and }|A|=k\}.

Place an edge between distinct vertices (x,y)(x,y) and (x′,y′)(x^{\prime},y^{\prime}) if |x−x′|≤1|x-x^{\prime}|\leq 1 and |y−y′|≤1|y-y^{\prime}|\leq 1.

As an example, the vertex set V6V_{6} is shown in Figure 2. To prove Theorem 1.7, we will show inductively that for k≥3k\geq 3, the vertices (2​k,3​k)(2k,3k) and ((k+12),(k+23))\big(\binom{k+1}{2},\binom{k+2}{3}\big) are connected in 𝒢k\mathcal{G}_{k}; an example path is shown in Figure 2. Before starting the induction, we must prove that a particular part of the path between these vertices exists.

Lemma 3.2.

For k≥4k\geq 4, the points (2​k,3​k)(2k,3k) and (3​k−2,6​k−5)(3k-2,6k-5) are connected by a path in 𝒢k\mathcal{G}_{k}.

Proof.

We will explicitly construct a path 𝒫\mathcal{P} from (2​k,3​k)(2k,3k) to (3​k−2,6​k−5)(3k-2,6k-5). Define

Aa={0}∪[2,k−1]∪{k+a},Bb=[0,1]∪[3,k−1]∪{k+b}.A_{a}=\{0\}\cup[2,k-1]\cup\{k+a\},\;B_{b}=[0,1]\cup[3,k-1]\cup\{k+b\}.

Then explicit computations yield that

g⁡(Aa)=(|2​Aa|,|3​Aa|)={(2​k+a,3​k+2​a) if ​0≤a≤k−3(3​k−3,5​k−5) if ​a=k−2(3​k−2,4​k−2+a) if ​k−1≤a≤2​k−4(3​k−2,6​k−5) if ​a=2​k−2,g(A_{a})=(|2A_{a}|,|3A_{a}|)=\begin{cases}(2k+a,3k+2a)&\text{ if }0\leq a\leq k-3\\ (3k-3,5k-5)&\text{ if }a=k-2\\ (3k-2,4k-2+a)&\text{ if }k-1\leq a\leq 2k-4\\ (3k-2,6k-5)&\text{ if }a=2k-2,\end{cases}

and

g⁡(Bb)=(|2​Bb|,|3​Bb|)={(2​k+1+b,3​k+1+2​b) if ​0≤b≤k−4(3​k−2,5​k−4) if b=k−2,k>4.g(B_{b})=(|2B_{b}|,|3B_{b}|)=\begin{cases}(2k+1+b,3k+1+2b)&\text{ if }0\leq b\leq k-4\\ (3k-2,5k-4)&\text{ if }b=k-2,k>4.\end{cases}

Also, define B2′={0,1,4,5}B_{2}^{\prime}=\{0,1,4,5\}, and compute g⁡(B2′)=(9,16)g(B_{2}^{\prime})=(9,16). Let Bk−2∗B_{k-2}^{*} denote Bk−2B_{k-2} if k>4k>4 and B2′B_{2}^{\prime} if k=4k=4. Using the notation g⁡(C1,…,Cn)=g⁡(C1),…,g⁡(Cn)g(C_{1},\ldots,C_{n})=g(C_{1}),\ldots,g(C_{n}), then we can check that

𝒫=g⁡(A0,B0,A1,B1,…,Ak−4,Bk−4,Ak−3,Ak−2,Bk−2∗,Ak−1,Ak,Ak+1,…,A2​k−5,A2​k−4,A2​k−2)\mathcal{P}=g(A_{0},B_{0},A_{1},B_{1},\ldots,A_{k-4},B_{k-4},A_{k-3},A_{k-2},B_{k-2}^{*},A_{k-1},A_{k},A_{k+1},\ldots,A_{2k-5},A_{2k-4},A_{2k-2})

gives a path from (2​k,3​k)(2k,3k) to (3​k−2,6​k−5)(3k-2,6k-5) in 𝒢k\mathcal{G}_{k}, as desired. ∎

We are now ready to prove Theorem 1.7 by inducting on kk, with inductive hypothesis the existence of a path between (2​k,3​k)(2k,3k) and ((k+12),(k+23))\big(\binom{k+1}{2},\binom{k+2}{3}\big) in 𝒢k\mathcal{G}_{k}.

Proof of Theorem 1.7.

We induct on kk. Our inductive hypothesis is that the vertices (2​k,3​k)(2k,3k) and ((k+12),(k+23))\big(\binom{k+1}{2},\binom{k+2}{3}\big) are connected by a path in 𝒢k\mathcal{G}_{k}. To prove Theorem 1.7 from this, it suffices to consider a path 𝒫\mathcal{P} from (2​k,3​k)(2k,3k) to ((k+12),(k+23))\big(\binom{k+1}{2},\binom{k+2}{3}\big). Looking at the yy-values of the vertices in 𝒫\mathcal{P} implies that [3​k,(k+23)]⊆ℛ⁡(3,k)\left[3k,\binom{k+2}{3}\right]\subseteq\mathcal{R}(3,k). Combining this with Theorem 1.3, which excludes 3​k−13k-1 from ℛ⁡(3,k)\mathcal{R}(3,k), proves Theorem 1.7.

The base case is k=3k=3, where it is easy to check that g⁡({0,1,3})g(\{0,1,3\}) and g⁡({0,1,4})g(\{0,1,4\}) form a path from (6,9)(6,9) to (6,10)(6,10) in 𝒢3\mathcal{G}_{3}. Now, let k>3k>3. By the inductive hypothesis, assume that (2​(k−1),3​(k−1))(2(k-1),3(k-1)) and ((k2),(k+13))\big(\binom{k}{2},\binom{k+1}{3}\big) are connected in 𝒢k−1\mathcal{G}_{k-1}. We will show that (2​k,3​k)(2k,3k) and ((k+12),(k+23))\big(\binom{k+1}{2},\binom{k+2}{3}\big) are connected in 𝒢k\mathcal{G}_{k}.

Let A⊆[0,d]A\subseteq[0,d] be a set with |A|=k−1|A|=k-1 and 0,d∈A0,d\in A. Define A1=A∪{3​d}A_{1}=A\cup\{3d\} and A2=A∪{3​d+1}A_{2}=A\cup\{3d+1\} to be sets with |A1|=|A2|=k|A_{1}|=|A_{2}|=k. Then

3​A2=3​A∪(3​d+1+2​A)∪(6​d+2+A)∪{9​d+3}.3A_{2}=3A\cup(3d+1+2A)\cup(6d+2+A)\cup\{9d+3\}. (3.1)

Since h​A⊆[0,h​d]hA\subseteq[0,hd] for h∈{1,2,3}h\in\{1,2,3\}, these four sets are disjoint and

|3​A2|=|3​A|+|2​A|+(k−1)+1=|3​A|+|2​A|+k.|3A_{2}|=|3A|+|2A|+(k-1)+1=|3A|+|2A|+k.

With A2A_{2} replaced by A1A_{1}, we have

3​A1=3​A∪(3​d+2​A)∪(6​d+A)∪{9​d}.3A_{1}=3A\cup(3d+2A)\cup(6d+A)\cup\{9d\}.

These four sets overlap in exactly one place, since 3​d∈3​A∩(3​d+2​A)3d\in 3A\cap(3d+2A). So

|3​A1|=|3​A|+|2​A|+k−1.|3A_{1}|=|3A|+|2A|+k-1.

By similar logic, we can check that

|2​A1|=|2​A2|=|2​A|+k.|2A_{1}|=|2A_{2}|=|2A|+k.

for any a∈[1,n1−1].a\in[1,n_{1}-1].

Define Ixi≔f([1,n1]×⋯×[1,ni−1]×{xi}×{yi+1}×⋯×{yd})I_{x_{i}}\coloneq f([1,n_{1}]\times\cdots\times[1,n_{i-1}]\times\{x_{i}\}\times\{y_{i+1}\}\times\cdots\times\{y_{d}\}) for xi∈[1,ni]x_{i}\in[1,n_{i}], which is an interval by our inductive hypothesis. Then

f([1,n1]×⋯×[1,ni−1]×[1,ni]×{yi+1}×⋯×{yd})=⋃a=1niIa.f([1,n_{1}]\times\cdots\times[1,n_{i-1}]\times[1,n_{i}]\times\{y_{i+1}\}\times\cdots\times\{y_{d}\})=\bigcup_{a=1}^{n_{i}}I_{a}. (4.4)

Since ff is nonincreasing in each entry, min⁡Ia≥min⁡Ia+1\min I_{a}\geq\min I_{a+1} for all a∈[1,ni−1]a\in[1,n_{i}-1]. Also, by the definitions of δi\delta_{i} and Δi−1\Delta_{i-1}, we have

f⁡(1,1,1,…,ni−1,a,yi+1,…,yd)≤f⁡(1,1,1,…,1,a+1,yi+1,…,yd)+δi−Δi−1.f(1,1,1,\ldots,n_{i-1},a,y_{i+1},\ldots,y_{d})\leq f(1,1,1,\ldots,1,a+1,y_{i+1},\ldots,y_{d})+\delta_{i}-\Delta_{i-1}.

The value of ff on the left side is in IaI_{a} and the value of ff on the right side is in Ia+1I_{a+1}. Since δi−Δi−1≤0\delta_{i}-\Delta_{i-1}\leq 0, we have min⁡Ia≤max⁡Ia+1\min I_{a}\leq\max I_{a+1}. Hence, IaI_{a} and Ia+1I_{a+1} overlap. So both sides of (4.4) are intervals, and we are done. ∎

4.3.2 Disjoint Unions and Generating Functions

First, we note that working in ℤ\mathbb{Z} and ℤr\mathbb{Z}^{r} are equivalent.

Lemma 4.6.

For η,r,κ∈ℕ\eta,r,\kappa\in\mathbb{N}, we have

{(|A|,|2​A|,…,|η​A|):A⊂ℤr​ and ​|A|=κ}={(|A|,|2​A|,…,|η​A|):A⊂ℤ​ and ​|A|=κ}.\{(|A|,|2A|,\ldots,|\eta A|):A\subset\mathbb{Z}^{r}\textnormal{ and }|A|=\kappa\}=\{(|A|,|2A|,\ldots,|\eta A|):A\subset\mathbb{Z}\textnormal{ and }|A|=\kappa\}.
Proof.

We induct on rr. With r=1r=1 this is trivial. Given A⊂ℤrA\subset\mathbb{Z}^{r}, let M=max⁡{‖a‖∞:a∈A}M=\max\{\|a\|_{\infty}:a\in A\}. Define a function ϕ:ℤr→ℤr−1\phi:\mathbb{Z}^{r}\to\mathbb{Z}^{r-1} to be the linear map which takes (x1,…,xr−1,0)→(x1,…,xr−1)(x_{1},\ldots,x_{r-1},0)\to(x_{1},\ldots,x_{r-1}) and takes (0,0,…,0,1)↦(⌈3​η​M⌉,0,0,…,0){(0,0,\ldots,0,1)\mapsto(\lceil 3\eta M\rceil,0,0,\ldots,0)}. Let A′=ϕ⁡(A)A^{\prime}=\phi(A). It is easy to check that ϕ\phi is a Freiman isomorphism of order η\eta, so we have |i​A′|=|i​A||iA^{\prime}|=|iA| for 1≤i≤η1\leq i\leq\eta. ∎

We now define a disjoint union of sets and a generating function.

Definition 4.7.

Let A⊂ℤrA\subset\mathbb{Z}^{r} and B⊂ℤsB\subset\mathbb{Z}^{s} with |A|=a|A|=a and |B|=b|B|=b. Define the disjoint union A⊔BA\sqcup B as the set of a+ba+b points in ℤr+s+2\mathbb{Z}^{r+s+2} given by

A⊔B=(A,0,1,0)∪(0,B,0,1)⊂ℤr×ℤs×ℤ×ℤ.A\sqcup B=(A,0,1,0)\cup(0,B,0,1)\subset\mathbb{Z}^{r}\times\mathbb{Z}^{s}\times\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}.
Definition 4.8.

Define 0​A={0}0A=\{0\}. For A⊂ℤrA\subset\mathbb{Z}^{r} finite, define the generating function

ℱA​(z)≔∑η=0∞|η​A|​zη.\mathcal{F}_{A}(z)\coloneq\sum_{\eta=0}^{\infty}|\eta A|z^{\eta}.

We now prove that the generating function behaves multiplicatively with respect to disjoint unions.

Lemma 4.9.

For A⊂ℤrA\subset\mathbb{Z}^{r} and B⊂ℤsB\subset\mathbb{Z}^{s} finite,

ℱA⊔B​(z)=ℱA​(z)⋅ℱB​(z).\mathcal{F}_{A\sqcup B}(z)=\mathcal{F}_{A}(z)\cdot\mathcal{F}_{B}(z).
Proof.

Elements of η⁡(A⊔B)\eta(A\sqcup B) are formed by adding up ii elements from (A,0,1,0)(A,0,1,0) and η−i\eta-i elements from (0,B,0,1)(0,B,0,1), which yields |i​A|​|(η−i)​B||iA||(\eta-i)B| possible sums. Sums of η\eta elements with different values of ii cannot be equal, since they will differ in their last two coordinates. Varying the value of ii between 00 and η\eta gives

|η⁡(A⊔B)|=|η​A|+|(η−1)​A|​|B|+|(η−2)​A​||2​B|+⋯+|​η​B|,|\eta(A\sqcup B)|=|\eta A|+|(\eta-1)A||B|+|(\eta-2)A||2B|+\cdots+|\eta B|,

so we are done by applying Definition 4.8. ∎

Notice that ℱA⊔(B⊔C)​(z)=ℱ(A⊔B)⊔C​(z)\mathcal{F}_{A\sqcup(B\sqcup C)}(z)=\mathcal{F}_{(A\sqcup B)\sqcup C}(z). Whenever taking a disjoint union of more than two sets, we do so in an arbitrary order, as in such circumstances we will only care about the data in the generating function, which we know to be equal. In particular, with A=⨆i=1mAiA=\displaystyle\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{m}{A_{i}}, we have

ℱA​(z)=∏i=1mℱAi​(z).\mathcal{F}_{A}(z)=\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathcal{F}_{A_{i}}(z).

Recall that hh is fixed; we now consider asymptotics as kk grows to infinity. Given a function f:ℕ→ℤf:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{Z} and i∈ℝ≥0i\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}, we let the expressions f⁡(a)∈O⁡(ai)f(a)\in O(a^{i}) and f⁡(a)∈Θ⁡(ai)f(a)\in\Theta(a^{i})11 1 If i<0i<0 then f⁡(a)∈O⁡(ai)f(a)\in O(a^{i}) or Θ⁡(ai)\Theta(a^{i}) if f⁡(a)=0f(a)=0 for all a∈ℕa\in\mathbb{N}. have their usual meanings. Say that f⁡(a)∈Θ+​(ai)f(a)\in\Theta_{+}(a^{i}) if f⁡(a)∈Θ⁡(ai)f(a)\in\Theta(a^{i}) and there is some a0∈ℕa_{0}\in\mathbb{N} such that f⁡(a)>0f(a)>0 if a>a0a>a_{0}. Now, we define the notions of O⁡[[⋅]]O[[\cdot]] and Θ+​[[⋅]]\Theta_{+}[[\cdot]] and ≡\equiv that we will use to approximate the sizes of generating functions.

Definition 4.10.

We say that a power series ℱ⁡(z)=1+a1​z+a2​z2+a3​z3+⋯\mathcal{F}(z)=1+a_{1}z+a_{2}z^{2}+a_{3}z^{3}+\cdots is in O⁡[[a​z]]O[[az]] (respectively Θ+​[[a​z]]\Theta_{+}[[az]]) if ai∈O⁡(ai)a_{i}\in O(a^{i}) (respectively Θ+​(ai)\Theta_{+}(a^{i})) for i≤hi\leq h. For 𝒢⁡(z)=1+b1​z+b2​z2+b3​z3+⋯\mathcal{G}(z)=1+b_{1}z+b_{2}z^{2}+b_{3}z^{3}+\cdots another power series, we say ℱ⁡(z)≡𝒢⁡(z)\mathcal{F}(z)\equiv\mathcal{G}(z) if ai=bia_{i}=b_{i} for all i≤hi\leq h.

Note that for ℱ⁡(z)∈O⁡[[a​z]]\mathcal{F}(z)\in O[[az]] or Θ+​[[a​z]]\Theta_{+}[[az]], we require ℱ⁡(z)\mathcal{F}(z) to have constant term a0=1a_{0}=1. We now state a lemma about how the sizes of power series vary under multiplication.

Lemma 4.11.

Fix r∈ℕr\in\mathbb{N}. If ℱ⁡(z)∈Θ+​[[a​z]]\mathcal{F}(z)\in\Theta_{+}[[az]] and b=o⁡(a)b=o(a) and 𝒢(j)​(z)∈O⁡[[b​z]]\mathcal{G}^{(j)}(z)\in O[[bz]] for all j∈[1,r]j\in[1,r], then

𝒫⁡(z)≔ℱ⁡(z)⋅∏j=1r𝒢(j)​(z)∈Θ+​[[a​z]].\mathcal{P}(z)\coloneq\mathcal{F}(z)\cdot\prod_{j=1}^{r}\mathcal{G}^{(j)}(z)\in\Theta_{+}[[az]].
Proof.

We induct on rr. First let r=1r=1. Let ℱ⁡(z)=1+a1​z+a2​z2+a3​z3+⋯\mathcal{F}(z)=1+a_{1}z+a_{2}z^{2}+a_{3}z^{3}+\cdots for ai∈Θ+​(ai)a_{i}\in\Theta_{+}(a^{i}). Let 𝒢(1)​(z)=1+b1​z+b2​z2+b3​z3+⋯\mathcal{G}^{(1)}(z)=1+b_{1}z+b_{2}z^{2}+b_{3}z^{3}+\cdots for bi∈O⁡(bi)b_{i}\in O(b^{i}). Let 𝒫⁡(z)=1+p1​z+p2​z2+p3​z3+⋯\mathcal{P}(z)=1+p_{1}z+p_{2}z^{2}+p_{3}z^{3}+\cdots. For η≤h\eta\leq h, we have

pη=∑ν=0ηaν​bη−ν.p_{\eta}=\sum_{\nu=0}^{\eta}a_{\nu}b_{\eta-\nu}.

The fastest growing term will be aη∈Θ+​(aη)a_{\eta}\in\Theta_{+}(a^{\eta}). All other terms will be in O⁡(aη)⋅baO(a^{\eta})\cdot\frac{b}{a}, and will thus be dwarfed by aηa_{\eta}. Thus, pη∈Θ+​(aη)p_{\eta}\in\Theta_{+}(a^{\eta}).

Now, assume the statement is true for r−1r-1. Let

𝒫′​(z)≔ℱ⁡(z)⋅∏j=1r−1𝒢(j)​(z)∈Θ+​[[a​z]]\mathcal{P}^{\prime}(z)\coloneq\mathcal{F}(z)\cdot\prod_{j=1}^{r-1}\mathcal{G}^{(j)}(z)\in\Theta_{+}[[az]]

by the inductive hypothesis. By repeating the argument of r=1r=1 on 𝒫⁡(z)=𝒫′​(z)​𝒢(r)​(z)\mathcal{P}(z)=\mathcal{P}^{\prime}(z)\mathcal{G}^{(r)}(z), we get that 𝒫⁡(z)∈Θ+​[[a​z]]\mathcal{P}(z)\in\Theta_{+}[[az]]. ∎

4.3.3 Sumset Sizes of Bj,ℓB_{j,\ell}, Sm,ℓS_{m,\ell}, and Tm,ℓT_{m,\ell}

We begin with our construction of dense sets Bj,ℓB_{j,\ell}, which are given by the union of an arithmetic progression and an integer, and state their properties.

Definition 4.12.

Let ℓ≥3\ell\geq 3, and s=(h−1)​(ℓ−2)+1s=(h-1)(\ell-2)+1. Define the set Bj,ℓ≔[0,ℓ−2]∪{h⁡(ℓ−2)+2−j}B_{j,\ell}\coloneq[0,\ell-2]\cup\{h(\ell-2)+2-j\} for j∈[1,s]j\in[1,s].

Lemma 4.13.

For ℓ≥3\ell\geq 3, the sets B1,ℓ,…,Bs,ℓB_{1,\ell},\ldots,B_{s,\ell} satisfy the following:

  1. (a)

    0≤|η​Bj−1,ℓ|−|η​Bj,ℓ|≤h0\leq|\eta B_{j-1,\ell}|-|\eta B_{j,\ell}|\leq h for all j∈[2,s]j\in[2,s] and η∈[2,h]\eta\in[2,h];

  2. (b)

    |η​Bj,ℓ|<h2​ℓ|\eta B_{j,\ell}|<h^{2}\ell for all j∈[1,s]j\in[1,s] and η∈[2,h]\eta\in[2,h];

  3. (c)

    ℱB1,3​(z)≡(1−z)−3.\mathcal{F}_{B_{1,3}}(z)\equiv(1-z)^{-3}.

  4. (d)

    If ℓ>3\ell>3, then ℱB1,ℓ​(z)≡(1−z)−1​ℱBs,ℓ−1​(z).\mathcal{F}_{B_{1,\ell}}(z)\equiv(1-z)^{-1}\mathcal{F}_{B_{s,\ell-1}}(z).

Proof.

An exact formula for |η​Bj,ℓ||\eta B_{j,\ell}|, due to [Lev96], is given in (2.2). This immediately implies (a). For (b), notice that Bj,ℓ⊆[0,h⁡(ℓ−1)]B_{j,\ell}\subseteq[0,h(\ell-1)] and η≤h\eta\leq h, so η​Bj,ℓ⊆[0,h2​(ℓ−1)]\eta B_{j,\ell}\subseteq[0,h^{2}(\ell-1)]. Therefore |η​Bj,ℓ|<h2​ℓ|\eta B_{j,\ell}|<h^{2}\ell. For (c), the binomial theorem gives (1−z)−3=∑η=0∞(η+22)​zη(1-z)^{-3}=\sum_{\eta=0}^{\infty}\binom{\eta+2}{2}z^{\eta}. By definition, B1,3={0,1,h+1}B_{1,3}=\{0,1,h+1\}. For 1≤η≤h1\leq\eta\leq h, the identity |η​B1,3|=(η+22)|\eta B_{1,3}|=\binom{\eta+2}{2} follows from setting qq to be hh and hh to be η\eta and kk to be 3 in (2.2).

For part (d), let d=h⁡(ℓ−2)+1d=h(\ell-2)+1. Then Bs,ℓ−1=[0,ℓ−2]B_{s,\ell-1}=[0,\ell-2] and B1,ℓ=[0,ℓ−2]∪{d}B_{1,\ell}=[0,\ell-2]\cup\{d\}. Let η∈[1,h]\eta\in[1,h]. In a similar way to (3.1),

η​B1,ℓ=⋃ν=0η((η−ν)​d+ν​Bs,ℓ−1).\eta B_{1,\ell}=\bigcup_{\nu=0}^{\eta}\big((\eta-\nu)d+\nu B_{s,\ell-1}\big). (4.5)

Since d>h⁡(ℓ−2)d>h(\ell-2), the sets on the right side of (4.5) are disjoint, so |η​B1,ℓ|=∑ν=0η|ν​Bs,ℓ−1||\eta B_{1,\ell}|=\sum_{\nu=0}^{\eta}|\nu B_{s,\ell-1}|. Plugging in that (1−z)−1=(1+z+z2+⋯)(1-z)^{-1}=(1+z+z^{2}+\cdots) yields (d). ∎

Now, we define a set Sm,ℓS_{m,\ell} to be a geometric series which includes 0, has common ratio mm, and has ℓ\ell elements. We then bound its generating function ℱSm,ℓ​(z)\mathcal{F}_{S_{m,\ell}}(z).

Definition 4.14.

For m≥2m\geq 2 and ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2, define the set Sm,ℓ≔{0,1,m,m2,…,mℓ−2}S_{m,\ell}\coloneq\{0,1,m,m^{2},\ldots,m^{\ell-2}\}.

Lemma 4.15.

For m≥2m\geq 2 and ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2, we have

ℱSm,ℓ​(z)=1−(ℓ−2)​zm​O​[[ℓ​z]](1−z)ℓ.\mathcal{F}_{S_{m,\ell}}(z)=\frac{1-(\ell-2)z^{m}O[[\ell z]]}{(1-z)^{\ell}}.
Proof.

Let η∈ℕ\eta\in\mathbb{N}. The elements in η​Sm,ℓ\eta S_{m,\ell} can be viewed as numbers nn where ⌊nmℓ−2⌋\lfloor\frac{n}{m^{\ell-2}}\rfloor plus the sum of the base-mm digits of n(modmℓ−2)n\pmod{m^{\ell-2}} is less than or equal to η\eta. To construct such an nn, construct nn with ⌊nmℓ−2⌋\lfloor\frac{n}{m^{\ell-2}}\rfloor copies of mℓ−2m^{\ell-2}, and then use the base expansion of n(modmℓ−2)n\pmod{m^{\ell-2}} in base mm. This is a general construction of all elements nn in η​Sm,ℓ\eta S_{m,\ell}.

This gives an expression of |η​Sm,ℓ||\eta S_{m,\ell}| as the number of ways to put η\eta balls in ℓ\ell boxes, where ℓ−2\ell-2 of the boxes have a maximum number of m−1m-1 balls, and 22 of the boxes have no maximum. The ℓ−2\ell-2 boxes correspond to the number of 11’s, mm’s, …\ldots, mℓ−3m^{\ell-3}’s in the base-mm expansion of nn. These numbers are bounded between 00 and m−1m-1. One infinite-capacity box corresponds to the number of mℓ−2m^{\ell-2}’s in nn, and the other corresponds to the ‘overflow’, or the number of 00’s in nn. In total, nn must be formed by exactly η\eta balls, as it is a sum of η\eta elements of Sm,ℓS_{m,\ell}. This gives a generating function formula

ℱSm,ℓ​(z)=(1+z+z2+⋯+zm−1)ℓ−2​(1+z+z2+⋯)2=(1−zm)ℓ−2(1−z)ℓ.\mathcal{F}_{S_{m,\ell}}(z)=(1+z+z^{2}+\cdots+z^{m-1})^{\ell-2}(1+z+z^{2}+\cdots)^{2}=\frac{(1-z^{m})^{\ell-2}}{(1-z)^{\ell}}.

Expanding the numerator (1−zm)ℓ−2(1-z^{m})^{\ell-2} out using the binomial theorem yields the desired result. ∎

Now, we will define a similar set Tm,ℓT_{m,\ell}, which is a geometric series with common ratio mm and ℓ\ell elements which does not include 0. With a bit more work, we prove a similar result about the generating function ℱTm,ℓ​(z)\mathcal{F}_{T_{m,\ell}}(z).

Definition 4.16.

For m≥2m\geq 2 and ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2, define the set Tm,ℓ≔{1,m,m2,…,mℓ−1}=Sm,ℓ+1∖{0}.T_{m,\ell}\coloneq\{1,m,m^{2},\ldots,m^{\ell-1}\}=S_{m,\ell+1}\setminus\{0\}.

Lemma 4.17.

For m≥2m\geq 2 and ℓ≥2\ell\geq 2, we have

ℱTm,ℓ​(z)=1−(ℓ−12)​zm+1​O​[[ℓ​z]](1−z)ℓ.\mathcal{F}_{T_{m,\ell}}(z)=\frac{1-\binom{\ell-1}{2}z^{m+1}O[[\ell z]]}{(1-z)^{\ell}}.
Proof.

Let η∈ℕ\eta\in\mathbb{N}. We will approximate |η​Tm,ℓ||\eta T_{m,\ell}| by putting sums of elements of Tm,ℓT_{m,\ell} into a standardized form. Say that a representation n=a0+a1​m+a2​m2+⋯+aℓ−1​mℓ−1n=a_{0}+a_{1}m+a_{2}m^{2}+\cdots+a_{\ell-1}m^{\ell-1} is in rr-normal form if a0,…,aℓ−2a_{0},\ldots,a_{\ell-2} are in [0,m−1][0,m-1] and aℓ−1≥0a_{\ell-1}\geq 0 and a0+⋯+aℓ−1=ra_{0}+\cdots+a_{\ell-1}=r. By taking the base-mm expansion of nn, every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} can be written in normal form uniquely.

Each element n∈η​Tm,ℓn\in\eta T_{m,\ell} can be written as n=a0+a1​m+a2​m2+⋯+aℓ−1​mℓ−1n=a_{0}+a_{1}m+a_{2}m^{2}+\cdots+a_{\ell-1}m^{\ell-1}, where ai≥0a_{i}\geq 0 and a0+⋯+aℓ−1=ηa_{0}+\cdots+a_{\ell-1}=\eta. This representation of nn might not be unique, so we will put nn into normal form. If ai≥ma_{i}\geq m for some i<ℓ−1i<\ell-1, we can decrement aia_{i} by mm and add 11 to ai+1a_{i+1} without changing the value of nn; after this procedure then a0+⋯+aℓ−1=η−(m−1)a_{0}+\cdots+a_{\ell-1}=\eta-(m-1). Iterating this whenever possible, we will eventually get that a0,…,aℓ−2a_{0},\ldots,a_{\ell-2} are in [0,m−1][0,m-1] and aℓ−1a_{\ell-1} is any nonnegative integer; if we have done this jj times, we get the sum a0+⋯+aℓ−1=η−j⁡(m−1)a_{0}+\cdots+a_{\ell-1}=\eta-j(m-1). Thus, any element n∈η​Tm,ℓn\in\eta T_{m,\ell} can be put into η−j⁡(m−1)\eta-j(m-1)-normal form for some j≥0j\geq 0, and this form is unique.

Now, we reverse this process. Consider an element nn in η−j⁡(m−1)\eta-j(m-1)-normal form. To pull back nn into η​Tm,ℓ\eta T_{m,\ell}, we need to decrement aia_{i} by 1 and increment ai−1a_{i-1} by mm for jj different nonzero values of ii. This is possible as long as we never reach a state where ai=0a_{i}=0 for all i>0i>0, which would mean nn is represented as a sum of η−j′​(m−1)\eta-j^{\prime}(m-1) copies of 1. This will only happen when n=η−j′​(m−1)n=\eta-j^{\prime}(m-1) for j′≥1j^{\prime}\geq 1. This rules out ⌊ηm−1⌋\lfloor\frac{\eta}{m-1}\rfloor numbers. Therefore, |η​Tm,ℓ||\eta T_{m,\ell}| is equal to the number of elements nn in η−j⁡(m−1)\eta-j(m-1)-normal form for any j≥0j\geq 0, minus ⌊ηm−1⌋\lfloor\frac{\eta}{m-1}\rfloor.

We now create the generating function ℱTm,ℓ\mathcal{F}_{T_{m,\ell}}. Elements in rr-normal form can be counted as the number of ways to put rr balls in ℓ\ell boxes, where the number of balls in box ii corresponds to aia_{i}. There are ℓ−1\ell-1 boxes which have a maximum of m−1m-1 balls, and 11 box with no maximum number of balls. Then, multiplying by (1+zm−1+z2​(m−1)+⋯)(1+z^{m-1}+z^{2(m-1)}+\cdots) to account for elements in η−j⁡(m−1)\eta-j(m-1)-normal form, and subtracting ⌊ηm−1⌋\lfloor\frac{\eta}{m-1}\rfloor, gives the generating function:

ℱTm,ℓ​(z)\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{T_{m,\ell}}(z) =(1+z+z2+⋯+zm−1)ℓ−1​(1+z+z2+⋯)​(1+zm−1+z2​(m−1)+⋯)−∑η=0∞⌊ηm−1⌋​zη\displaystyle=(1+z+z^{2}+\cdots+z^{m-1})^{\ell-1}(1+z+z^{2}+\cdots)(1+z^{m-1}+z^{2(m-1)}+\cdots)-\sum_{\eta=0}^{\infty}\left\lfloor\frac{\eta}{m-1}\right\rfloor z^{\eta}
=(1−zm)ℓ−1(1−z)ℓ​(1−zm−1)−∑η=0∞⌊ηm−1⌋​zη.\displaystyle=\frac{(1-z^{m})^{\ell-1}}{(1-z)^{\ell}(1-z^{m-1})}-\sum_{\eta=0}^{\infty}\left\lfloor\frac{\eta}{m-1}\right\rfloor z^{\eta}.

We can then simplify

∑η=0∞⌊ηm−1⌋​zη=zm−1​(1+z+z2+⋯)​(1+zm−1+z2​(m−1)+⋯)=zm−1(1−z)​(1−zm−1).\sum_{\eta=0}^{\infty}\left\lfloor\frac{\eta}{m-1}\right\rfloor z^{\eta}=z^{m-1}(1+z+z^{2}+\cdots)(1+z^{m-1}+z^{2(m-1)}+\cdots)=\frac{z^{m-1}}{(1-z)(1-z^{m-1})}.

Plugging this into our formula for ℱTm,ℓ​(z)\mathcal{F}_{T_{m,\ell}}(z) gives

ℱTm,ℓ​(z)=(1−zm)ℓ−1−zm−1​(1−z)ℓ−1(1−z)ℓ​(1−zm−1)=1−zm−1−(ℓ−12)​zm+1+∑i=3∞O⁡(ℓi)​zi+m−1(1−z)ℓ​(1−zm−1).\mathcal{F}_{T_{m,\ell}}(z)=\frac{(1-z^{m})^{\ell-1}-z^{m-1}(1-z)^{\ell-1}}{(1-z)^{\ell}(1-z^{m-1})}=\frac{1-z^{m-1}-\binom{\ell-1}{2}z^{m+1}+\sum_{i=3}^{\infty}O(\ell^{i})z^{i+m-1}}{(1-z)^{\ell}(1-z^{m-1})}.

Expanding the left side of this out for ℓ=2\ell=2 and the right side out for ℓ>2\ell>2 yields the desired result. ∎

4.3.4 Putting it All Together

We begin by defining a notion of a family of sets being connected.

Definition 4.18.

A set of sets 𝒜={A1,…,Ar}\mathcal{A}=\{A_{1},\ldots,A_{r}\} with all |Ai|=k|A_{i}|=k is connected if the set of sumset sizes h​𝒜≔{|h​A|:A∈𝒜}h\mathcal{A}\coloneq\{|hA|:A\in\mathcal{A}\} forms an interval.

Now, using all of our work in Section 4.3.3 to understand the component sets, we prove that the set of all AA, with bb fixed and j,sm,tm−1j,s_{m},t_{m-1} varying for m∈[3,h]m\in[3,h], is connected.

5 Future Directions

5.1 Working towards Conjecture 1.6

Let kh′k_{h}^{\prime} be the minimal natural number such that for all k>kh′k>k_{h}^{\prime}, we have

ℛ⁡(h,k)=[h​k−h+1,(h+k−1h)]∖Δh,k.\mathcal{R}(h,k)=\left[hk-h+1,\binom{h+k-1}{h}\right]\setminus\Delta_{h,k}. (5.1)

Then, Theorem 1.4 proves that kh′k_{h}^{\prime} exists, and by Remark 1.5, kh′≤220​h2k_{h}^{\prime}\leq 2^{20h^{2}}. Conjecture 1.6 is that kh′≤hk_{h}^{\prime}\leq h. It would be interesting to try to improve the upper bound on kh′k_{h}^{\prime} to exponential in hh, or polynomial in hh, in order to work towards Conjecture 1.6. Or, if these bounds were improved for small hh, it might be possible to explicitly compute that k4′=4k_{4}^{\prime}=4 or k5′=4k_{5}^{\prime}=4, which is what numerical data suggests. We pose the question of whether the set of all kk satisfying (5.1) is always a half-open interval given by [kh′+1,∞)[k_{h}^{\prime}+1,\infty).

Another natural follow-up would be to extend the inductive arguments from the proof of Theorem 1.7 to h=4h=4 or h=5h=5. This could be approached using geometric pictures like Figure 4. We have been unable to do this using the exact methods from Theorem 1.7 because it seems necessary to control |2​A||2A|, |3​A||3A|, and |4​A||4A| all at once.

One could also try to compute more data to support or disprove Conjecture 1.6 for small hh and kk. So far, we have used a computer to show that this conjecture holds for all (h,k)(h,k) satisfying h+k<12h+k<12. Our algorithm uses a brute force method; it enumerates all sets AA with |A|=k|A|=k and diam​(A)≤d\text{diam}(A)\leq d for some fixed dd and then computes |h​A||hA| for all of them. More clever or efficient algorithms might be able to find much more data to support or disprove Conjecture 1.6.

5.2 What if h≥kh\geq k?

Let a “gap” in ℛ⁡(h,k)\mathcal{R}(h,k) be a number in [h​k−h+1,(h+k−1h)]∖ℛ⁡(h,k)\left[hk-h+1,\binom{h+k-1}{h}\right]\setminus\mathcal{R}(h,k). For many pairs (h,k)(h,k) with h≥kh\geq k, there are gaps in ℛ⁡(h,k)\mathcal{R}(h,k) that are not in Δh,k\Delta_{h,k}; in other words, (5.1) does not hold. We pose the problem of studying where all of these gaps are for certain values of (h,k)(h,k) and proving that many of these other gaps exist.

One place to start would be Theorem 2.2, which is due to [Lev96]. If h>k+1h>k+1, similar methods to our proof of Theorem 1.3 with larger diameters yield other gaps in ℛ⁡(h,k)\mathcal{R}(h,k) outside Δh,k\Delta_{h,k}. For example, if diam⁡(A)≤2​k−3\mathrm{diam}(A)\leq 2k-3, then |h​A|≤h⁡(2​k−3)+1|hA|\leq h(2k-3)+1 and if diam⁡(A)≥2​k−2\mathrm{diam}(A)\geq 2k-2 then similar logic to (2.3) gives that |h​A|≥k−1+(h−1)​(2​k−2)=h⁡(2​k−3)+h−k+1|hA|\geq k-1+(h-1)(2k-2)=h(2k-3)+h-k+1. Combining these bounds yields that ℛ⁡(h,k)∩[h⁡(2​k−3)+2,h⁡(2​k−3)+h−k]=∅\mathcal{R}(h,k)\cap[h(2k-3)+2,h(2k-3)+h-k]=\emptyset. Similar analysis with larger values of diam⁡(A)\mathrm{diam}(A) and larger values of h−kh-k will yield more gaps.

With k=3k=3 and h≥4h\geq 4, Nathanson [Nat25c, Theorem 9] found the exact form of ℛ⁡(h,k)\mathcal{R}(h,k), showing there are many more gaps in ℛ⁡(h,k)\mathcal{R}(h,k). With k=4k=4 and h≥4h\geq 4, experimental data suggests 5​h∉ℛ⁡(h,4)5h\not\in\mathcal{R}(h,4), which is an example of a conjectured gap. The only (conjectured) gaps in ℛ⁡(h,k)\mathcal{R}(h,k) outside Δh,k\Delta_{h,k} we have found with h≤k+1h\leq k+1 occur when (h,k)∈{(4,3),(4,4),(5,4)}(h,k)\in\{(4,3),(4,4),(5,4)\}. When hh is significantly larger than kk, there are many more gaps in ℛ⁡(h,k)\mathcal{R}(h,k) than can be explained by Theorem 2.2. One could conjecture where these other gaps occur, and try to prove that any of them exist.

5.3 Restricted Sumsets

For A⊂ℤA\subset\mathbb{Z}, define the hh-fold restricted sumset of AA by

h​A^≔{a1+⋯+ah:ai∈A​ and ​ai≠aj​ if ​i≠j}.\widehat{hA}\coloneq\{a_{1}+\cdots+a_{h}:a_{i}\in A\text{ and }a_{i}\neq a_{j}\text{ if }i\neq j\}.

Then, Nathanson defined ℛ^​(h,k)\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(h,k) analogously to ℛ⁡(h,k)\mathcal{R}(h,k).

Definition 5.1.

[Nat25c] Define the range of cardinalities of hh-fold restricted sumsets

ℛ^​(h,k)≔{|h​A^|:A⊂ℤ​ and ​|A|=k}.\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(h,k)\coloneq\{|\widehat{hA}|:A\subset\mathbb{Z}\text{ and }|A|=k\}.

All of the questions asked or answered in this paper about ℛ⁡(h,k)\mathcal{R}(h,k) can be asked about ℛ^​(h,k)\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(h,k), and one could study whether similar results to Theorems 1.3, 1.4, and 1.7 hold in this context.

5.4 Working with Torsion

The results in this paper also hold with ℤ\mathbb{Z} replaced by any infinite torsion-free abelian group. We pose the problem of determining the form of ℛ⁡(h,k)\mathcal{R}(h,k) or ℛ^​(h,k)\widehat{\mathcal{R}}(h,k) in groups with torsion. One interesting candidate for such a group is (ℤ/m​ℤ)n(\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z})^{n}, with m∈ℕ∖{1}m\in\mathbb{N}\setminus\{1\} and n∈ℕ∪{∞}n\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{\infty\}. This seems interesting already when m=2m=2.

5.5 Studying |h​A||hA| and |h′​A||h^{\prime}A| together

Another natural follow-up question is to try to figure out the exact form of the points in Figures 2 and 4. In particular, one can ask what all of the possible tuples (|h​A|,|h′​A|)(|hA|,|h^{\prime}A|) are, where A⊂ℤA\subset\mathbb{Z} and |A|=k|A|=k. With h=2h=2 and h′=3h^{\prime}=3, this is already a very difficult question, as illustrated in Figure 2. The Plunnecke–Ruzsa [Plü70, Ruz89] inequality gives a bound on where these points are found, but it is not close to tight. One could try to bound the points in a plot such as Figure 2 or Figure 4 between two curves, in a tight or nearly tight way. There are also many other questions that can be asked about the structure of the points in these plots; for example, in Figure 4 we can ask about the possible tuples (|3​A|,|4​A|)(|3A|,|4A|) if we fix |A||A| and |2​A||2A|, or about the possible tuples (|2​A|,|3​A|,|4​A|)(|2A|,|3A|,|4A|) if we fix |A||A|. All of these questions would be particularly interesting as kk gets large or in the limit as k→∞k\to\infty.

In graph theory, Razborov [Raz08] proved an inequality about the set of pairs of possible edge and triangle densities in a graph. The illustration of this in [Zha23, Figure 5.1] looks somewhat similar in character to Figure 2. It would be fascinating to see if there is a relation between the sets of possible tuples {(|{edges in ​G}|,|{triangles in ​G}|):G​ a graph with k vertices}\big\{\big(|\{\text{edges in }G\}|,|\{\text{triangles in }G\}|\big):G\text{ a graph with $k$ vertices}\big\} and {(|2​A|,|3​A|):A⊂ℤ​ and ​|A|=k}\{(|2A|,|3A|):A\subset\mathbb{Z}\text{ and }|A|=k\}.
